newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand sees volatile baht stabilising soon.
newsitem.headline: Thailand sees volatile baht stabilising soon.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Thursday he would announce a major economic package within two weeks that would help stabilise the volatile baht and bring down high Thai interest rates.
Thanong told reporters Thailand's sustained fiscal and monetary disciplines should help stabilise the baht which fell to a new record low against the dollar on Thursday morning.
The minister declined to reveal the package that would be unveiled but said it would be comprehensive in tackling what he called accumulated problems facing the country.
Thailand is going through its worst economic slump in over a decade with growth seen falling to around four percent this year from 6.4 percent in 1996.
The baht is under pressure, the finance and property sectors are riddled with liquidity and loan problems and exports have slowed sharply.

"Tackling these problems takes time...but the overall economic picture is not that bad. I am confident the current account deficit would be below six percent (of gross domestic product), inflation is not high and the (baht) exchange rate shows signs of stabilising," he said.

Thanong said it was normal for a newly floated currency to fluctuate. Thailand cut the baht loose into a new managed float regime on July 2 after pegging it to a dollar-dominated basket of currencies for about 13 years.
The baht plunged to its new low of 32.70 to the dollar in morning trade before it recovered to around 31.870 at midday on what dealers believed was due to central bank intervention.
The minister also said he expected current high Thai interest rates to ease in one or two months time.
Some major Thai banks this week raised their deposit and key lending rates.
Thai interest rates are among the highest in the region with the minimum lending rate ranging from 12.75-13.25 percent.
Asked if Thailand would seek financial support from the Bank of Japan to help overcome its financial woes, the minister said: "I could not tell you even if we planned to do that."
